claims.text: Grain-boundary decohesion can lead to brittle behavior in high-entropy alloys.
Grain-boundary nanoclustering can promote brittle behavior in high-entropy alloys.
Controlling alloy composition and microstructure can mitigate brittle behavior.
The proposed material begins as a single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Atom-probe tomography will characterize grain-boundary composition and microstructure.
The hypothesis is intended to apply at both high and low temperatures and under various loading conditions.
Grain-boundary sliding is a mechanism governing toughness degradation.
Dislocation structure is a mechanism governing toughness degradation.
The proposed intervention will improve toughness and resistance to brittle behavior.
Conventional alloys provide a baseline characterized by grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation.
The exact roles of grain-boundary decohesion, nanoclustering, and dislocation structure in high-entropy-alloy toughness degradation remain uncertain.
The experiment will compare high-entropy alloys having different grain-boundary compositions and microstructures across different temperatures and loading conditions.
Toughness, grain-boundary composition, microstructure, and dislocation structure will be measured.
A lack of correlation between grain-boundary decohesion or nanoclustering and brittle behavior would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts brittleness from decohesion and nanoclustering, but the stated intervention is only characterization rather than a composition or microstructure modification, so the predicted improvement in toughness does not follow from the intervention.
The mediator and mechanism are presented as degradation processes, while the predicted outcome is improved toughness; no mitigating change or causal step connecting them to improvement is specified.
